title: Make Time
author: Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky
thesisParagraph: Make Time argues that most people do not need a more punishing productivity system. They need a way to stop default forces from deciding the day before intention has a chance. The Busy Bandwagon pushes people toward visible busyness and instant responsiveness, while Infinity Pools offer endless low-friction distraction whenever attention gets tired. The book answers with a small daily operating loop: choose one Highlight, protect it with Laser, support attention through Energize, and use Reflect to learn what actually worked under real conditions.

coreIdeas.name: Defaults decide first
coreIdeas.oneSentence: A day often gets captured by work culture and endless inputs before a person has chosen what matters.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: notice which default force is taking command before blaming yourself in the abstract

coreIdeas.name: One chosen center beats vague intention
coreIdeas.oneSentence: A Highlight gives the day a center of gravity strong enough to compete with urgent and easy demands.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: pick one concrete outcome or moment that would make the day feel used well

coreIdeas.name: Attention needs friction around it
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Laser is not willpower; it is the redesign of devices, apps, and focus blocks so distraction has to work harder.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: make the next distraction less automatic before the focus block begins

coreIdeas.name: The body is part of focus
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Energy choices around movement, sleep, food, and caffeine change how available attention feels.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: treat physical state as a practical input to focus instead of a separate health virtue

coreIdeas.name: The system improves by evidence
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Reflect turns each day into a small experiment so tactics are refined, added, or dropped without drama.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: convert the day into one useful adjustment for tomorrow

targetReader: Busy knowledge workers, students, parents, makers, operators, and professionals who feel their days are full but strangely unclaimed, and who need a humane way to recover one meaningful part of each day without pretending every obligation can disappear.

signatureMoves: uses friendly design-sprint language around Highlight, Laser, Energize, and Reflect
keeps tactics small, testable, and forgiving
treats phones, calendars, and defaults as design materials
sounds like two product designers helping a busy friend run an experiment
avoidMoves: Avoid "The point is" as a paragraph hinge.
Avoid "the question is" as a setup crutch.
Avoid triadic abstract-noun lists such as clarity, courage, and resilience.
Do not make Make Time into monkish discipline.
Do not add heavy productivity machinery where a small default change is the point.

voiceAntiSpecimens: In this chapter, readers will explore a transformational productivity framework.
The authors argue that everyone can optimize their life through intentional behavior change.
Take a few moments to reflect deeply on your goals and unlock your best self.
The key insight is that focus is important in today's fast-paced digital world.
This principle can be applied holistically across work, school, relationships, and personal development.
teachingArc: The book begins by naming the default forces that steal command of the day. It then gives the reader a sequence of counter-moves: choose a single daily Highlight, protect attention long enough to work on it, restore the physical energy that makes focus possible, and review the evidence so tomorrow can be adjusted. The chapters compound from diagnosis to choice, from choice to protection, from protection to energy, and from energy to learning.
forbiddenMoves: Do not turn Make Time into generic time-blocking or task-list advice.
Do not make every problem a phone addiction problem; the Busy Bandwagon matters as much as Infinity Pools.
Do not promise total control over the day or total escape from modern work.
Do not turn Energize into medical or wellness claims beyond modest attention support.
Do not turn Reflect into elaborate tracking, scoring, or self-surveillance.
Do not confuse a Highlight with a full task list.
Do not make the method punitive when it is experimental.
